correlate.executive_summary: The assessment discovered multiple information-disclosure issues and an exposed application surface that increases attack surface. Reconnaissance identified WordPress endpoints (including a reachable /wp-login.php) and evidence that repository/configuration artifacts exist on the host (.env, .git/*, phpinfo.php). Several recommended security headers are not set. Network/service fingerprinting shows nginx on port 80 and an hcdn front-end on HTTPS; no product-version CVEs could be applied because the automated CVE lookup failed.

findings.title: Potentially sensitive files and repository artifacts discoverable (.env, .env.example, .git/config, .git/HEAD, phpinfo.php)
findings.evidence: recon: HTTP 403 responses observed on /.env, /.env.example, /.git/config, /.git/HEAD, /phpinfo.php that differ from baseline 404 responses (recon agent reported distinct 403 responses and included response-body hash c029d1c560ecb35b...). These responses indicate the presence of these files/paths even where direct access is denied.

findings.title: WordPress presence and accessible login endpoint (/wp-login.php, /wp-admin, /wp-content)
findings.evidence: recon: /wp-login.php returned HTTP 200 (body sha256=11e85ef11c4a137a...), /wp-admin and /wp-content returned HTTP 301 redirects — these responses differ from baseline 404 and indicate an active WordPress installation or WordPress routes.

findings.title: Missing security headers (Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy)
findings.evidence: recon: Responses from https://yashinfosec.com/ did not set strict-transport-security, x-content-type-options, x-frame-options or referrer-policy. nmap http-headers output (Server: hcdn, Cache-Control: no-store, alt-svc: ...) also does not show these headers.

findings.title: Server/service fingerprint: hcdn on HTTPS and nginx on HTTP
findings.evidence: nmap -sV detected http (nginx) on tcp/80 and https (hcdn) on tcp/443 (nmap). recon header hints also showed Server: hcdn.

findings.title: Open HTTP and HTTPS ports observed (80/tcp, 443/tcp)
findings.evidence: nmap: tcp/80 and tcp/443 in state=open (nmap -sV results).

findings.title: Contact email discovered in page content (http-grep output)
findings.evidence: nmap http-grep script output included 'email: info@example.com' on http://yashinfosec.com:80/ (nmap script http-grep).

findings.title: Summary of NSE script checks (automated checks returned no confirmed vulnerabilities)
findings.evidence: nmap: multiple NSE scripts ran (http-comments-displayer, http-csrf, http-stored-xss, http-dombased-xss, http-useragent-tester, etc.). Outputs either reported no issues (e.g. 'Couldn't find any comments/CSRF/stored XSS/DOM XSS') or failed to execute for some scripts (errors). No script produced a confirmed 'VULNERABLE' result or linked CVEs in the provided outputs.

correlate.deduplication_notes: Multiple recon entries reporting individual discoverable paths were combined into grouped findings: (1) sensitive/config artifacts (.env, .env.example, .git/config, .git/HEAD, phpinfo.php) and (2) WordPress-related endpoints (/wp-login.php, /wp-admin, /wp-content). The separate recon security-header findings were consolidated into a single 'Missing security headers' finding. The recon 'Technology fingerprint: hcdn' and the nmap server/banner detection of 'hcdn' were merged into one fingerprint finding. Nmap's many individual NSE script outputs were summarized into a single NSE-script summary finding. No CVEs were attached to any finding because the automated CVE lookup for the detected products (nginx, hcdn) failed; therefore CVE-based severity/confidence upgrades were not applied.
